by_task.when: Arizona law applies and the facts identify an item as medically or professionally prescribed assistive equipment for the debtor or a dependent.
by_task.procedure: Treat the item as a prescribed prosthetic or mobility aid under Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(9) and claim its full value because the supplied provision states no dollar cap.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify prescribed assistive equipment as ordinary household furniture merely because it is used in the home; do not apply this rule to ordinary furniture lacking the prescription or assistive condition.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and an asset fits a listed household-use category under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3), or is jewelry under § 522(d)(4).
by_task.procedure: Include § 522(d)(3) for listed household furnishings, goods, apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments, and include § 522(d)(4) separately for jewelry. A value above the statutory cap limits the amount but does not defeat eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry under § 522(d)(3), omit an otherwise eligible item because its value exceeds a cap, or extend either provision to property outside its listed category.

by_task.when: An asset is considered under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3) or is jewelry considered under § 522(d)(4).
by_task.procedure: First require that a § 522(d)(3) asset be one of the listed household-use categories, then assign no more than the lesser of its value and the $700 per-item limit. Evaluate jewelry separately under § 522(d)(4), using the lesser of value and $1,875 for one debtor. For jointly owned jewelry in a joint case, apply § 522(m) to each spouse's one-half interest and add the claims, each capped at $1,875.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the $14,875 aggregate ceiling as the claim for one item, classify jewelry under § 522(d)(3), or double § 522(d)(3)'s $700 cap for a particular jointly owned item.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and the debtor or a dependent uses real or personal property as a residence.
by_task.procedure: Include 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(1) as an applicable residence alternative even when the residence's value exceeds $27,900.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the $27,900 amount as an eligibility test or apply § 522(d)(1) to property that the facts do not identify as a residence, cooperative residence, or burial plot.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and an estate asset is being evaluated.
by_task.procedure: For every asset, evaluate 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) as a separate alternative, including property also eligible under § 522(d)(1), another category-specific federal provision, or an allowable state provision.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit the wildcard because another exemption applies, because the asset exceeds the wildcard ceiling, or because a residence is listed; do not add it when the supplied allowable jurisdictions exclude federal exemptions.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and an estate asset is being evaluated.
by_task.procedure: For 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5), calculate the independent claim as the lesser of the asset value and $1,475 plus up to $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1). When no residence consumes that amount, use a $15,425 ceiling for one debtor. In a joint case, apply § 522(m) separately to each spouse's equal interest and add the two claims, so the combined ceiling is $30,850.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not aggregate allocations across assets, displace other applicable alternatives, assume unused homestead capacity when the facts show it has been consumed, or apply the two-debtor ceiling to a single debtor.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the debtor owns personal property.
by_task.procedure: Add 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) as an independent alternative, including when a specific Illinois exemption also applies or the property's value exceeds $4,000.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat the $4,000 ceiling as an eligibility test, omit subsection (b) because subsection (a), (d), or (e) applies, or classify jewelry as necessary wearing apparel without facts establishing necessity.

by_task.when: Oregon law applies and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative even when the asset also fits a specific Oregon exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply it to real property or treat its $400 limit as a condition that makes a more valuable item ineligible.

by_task.when: Oregon law applies and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: For the independent Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) alternative, assign the lesser of the asset's value and $400.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not aggregate different assets or omit separately applicable Oregon exemptions.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania law applies to property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: For every property category, include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent alternative alongside any specific Pennsylvania or federal exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not restrict § 8123 to cash, omit it because another exemption applies, or use its $300-per-spouse limit as an eligibility test for more valuable property.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania law applies to property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: For the independent 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 alternative, assign the lesser of the property's value and $300.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not aggregate assets, replace a specific exemption, or exclude tangible property merely because the statute is titled a monetary exemption.
